Work & society · 13 min read

Japan’s highest-paid jobs are not the jobs people want most.

Pilots and doctors lead the salary table. Children choose bakeries and police work. University students choose companies. Adults choose stability. Put those rankings together and Japan’s idea of a “good job” becomes much more complicated.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published October 14, 2026 · Statistics checked October 14
PAY¥16.97mairline pilots
≠
DREAM11.7%pâtissier or baker among first graders

Editorial data graphic—not a photograph. Sources: MHLW 2024 wage survey; Dai-ichi Life 2025 first-grader survey.

Ask a Japanese child what job they want and the answer may smell like warm bread. Ask a university student where they want to work and the answer may be a furniture retailer, an airline or Sony. Ask an adult what makes work ideal and the most common answer is not prestige. It is stable income.

Then open the government wage table. At the top sits a job most people will never enter: aircraft pilot, averaging about ¥16.97 million in 2024. Doctors follow at roughly ¥13.38 million. University professors average about ¥10.93 million. The numbers are striking, but they do not predict Japan’s most desired careers. That mismatch is the real story.

How this ranking works. Japan figures are gross employee averages from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare’s 2024 Basic Survey on Wage Structure, calculated as monthly cash earnings × 12 plus annual bonuses. They are not starting salaries, take-home pay or guaranteed offers. Small occupational samples can move sharply; self-employed people and many executives are outside the comparison.

Japan’s high-pay table

RankOccupationEstimated annual gross payWhat the number hides
1Aircraft pilots¥16.97mSmall, highly selected workforce; licensing and irregular hours
2Doctors¥13.38mSpecialty, employer, age and on-call work vary enormously
3University professors¥10.93mSenior average; not the pay of a new academic
4University associate professors¥8.81mLong training pipeline and limited permanent posts
5Legal professionals¥7.65mBroad category; employee data do not describe every lawyer

The first surprise is age. A professor’s average reflects people who survived a long academic ladder; a 22-year-old cannot compare that figure with a graduate offer. The second is selection. Pilots combine rare licenses, responsibility and a small sample. Average occupational pay is partly a map of who remains in a profession long enough to be counted.

The third surprise is what is missing. A founder, celebrity or successful investor may earn more than everyone in the table, but “entrepreneur” is not a stable employee occupation with one meaningful average. Ranking jobs is not the same as ranking every way a person can become wealthy.

Why an American salary cannot simply be converted into yen

International salary lists often make one dramatic mistake: convert local pay at today’s exchange rate and declare a winner. That tells a traveler how much currency can be exchanged. It does not tell a resident what housing, health care, education, transport or retirement costs.

The OECD’s 2025 average-wage measure provides a consistent national benchmark: Japan ¥5.70 million, Britain £55,983, Germany €66,700, Norway NOK801,695, Australia A$108,674 and Canada C$92,401. These are modelled gross averages in national currency, not occupational figures. The United States also sits far above Japan in market-exchange-dollar comparisons. Purchasing-power conversion narrows the visual gap because prices differ, but it does not erase differences in productivity, hours, taxation or benefits.

United StatesSpecialist medicine and tech can pay exceptionally well; insurance and education costs change the lived result.
UK / Canada / AustraliaShared language does not mean one labour market; licensing and public-sector pay systems differ.
Germany / NorwayTaxes and social insurance fund benefits that a gross-salary ranking cannot price fairly.
Philippines / IraqUseful comparisons require national statistics and local purchasing power; OECD wage tables do not provide like-for-like coverage.

That last group deserves restraint. The Philippines and Iraq are important to Yuji’s audience, but forcing them into an OECD table would create false precision. Labour-force coverage, informal employment, occupation codes and currency conditions differ. The honest comparison is occupational status and relative pay within each country—not a single global league table assembled from incompatible websites.

The reveal: Japan has four different popularity rankings

For children, a job is something visible. Dai-ichi Life’s survey of 4,000 first graders found pâtissier or baker first overall at 11.7% in 2025. Police officer was rising. These choices are encounters: the person who makes a birthday cake, protects a street, teaches a class or scores a goal.

University students answer a different question. In the Mynavi–Nikkei ranking for students graduating in 2026, Nitori led humanities students for a third year; Sony Group led science students for a fourth. Airlines and travel companies rose among humanities students, while food and automotive businesses featured strongly in science. This is a ranking of employers, not occupations. A student may choose the organization before knowing the eventual role.

Adults produce a third ranking. In the Cabinet Office survey, 62.2% selected stable income as a feature of ideal work; 55.2% chose work–life balance; 54.2% chose enjoyable work. Using specialist ability followed at 36.4%, and avoiding damage to health at 35.2%. Respondents could select more than one answer. The result explains why the highest salary does not automatically win.

Mid-career workers create a fourth list. A 2025 survey of 900 employees aged 45–59 found that among those considering a move around retirement, 34% wanted different work and 26% wanted to use their skills elsewhere or independently. Salary matters, but so do autonomy, accumulated expertise and fear of losing status.

AGE 6–7Can I imagine doing it?Baker, police officer, athlete, teacher
UNIVERSITYCan I enter and grow there?Companies, brands, stability, assignment
MID-CAREERCan I use what I know?Transferable skill, balance, autonomy

How Japan differs from the “global standard”

There is no single world standard. Still, Japan has a distinctive feature: new graduates have traditionally joined a company as members of an intake rather than applying only for one sharply bounded occupation. Hiring is changing, and job-specific recruitment is expanding, but the company name remains unusually powerful in student rankings.

In the United States, Britain, Canada and Australia, graduate recruitment more often foregrounds a role, profession or program. Germany’s vocational system gives recognized occupations a clearer educational route. Norway combines high average pay with a broad welfare state. The Philippines sends many skilled workers into global labour markets, making overseas opportunity part of career calculation. Iraq’s public sector and oil economy create another set of incentives. These are tendencies, not national personalities, and they should never be used to predict an individual.

Across countries, children’s lists also reflect what society makes visible. Sports stars, doctors, teachers, police officers, creators and online personalities recur. But their order changes with media, gender norms, economic security and whether a profession feels reachable. A “dream job” survey measures imagination as much as demand.

What the salary table is actually good for

Use it to ask better questions. Is the figure a mean or median? Does it include bonuses and overtime? What is the average age? Are self-employed people included? How many hours are worked? What qualification bottleneck limits supply? A rank without those answers is entertainment, not career guidance.

For Japan, three gaps deserve attention: the gap between men’s and women’s pay, between regular and non-regular employment, and between metropolitan and regional opportunity. The 2025 MHLW preliminary survey put scheduled monthly pay for general workers at ¥340,600 overall, ¥373,400 for men and ¥285,900 for women. Different job distribution, tenure and leadership representation sit behind that ratio; the table does not establish one cause.

The word やりがい, yarigai, means the sense that work is worth doing. It combines yaru, to do, with gai, worth or value. Japanese career conversations often place it beside stability and pay, not instead of them. That is why the most revealing ranking is not “which job wins?” but “what does each generation believe work should give back?”

Walk through Japan with Yuji on TikTok LIVE and the occupations stop being rows: station staff, drivers, cooks, carers, teachers, engineers and shop workers become the systems holding an ordinary day together. DraMap, Yuji’s iOS game, turns Japanese such as shokugyō (occupation) and yarigai into language learned through play.

The highest-paid job answers one question. The job people choose answers what they believe a life should contain.
